0.title: Understanding People, Sharing the Gospel
0.overview:
Every person we meet is on a journey -- shaped by a worldview they may never have examined, carrying questions they may never have articulated, and longing for something they may not be able to name. Effective evangelism begins not with our message but with their world. We learn to listen before we speak, to understand before we explain, to love the person before we present the truth.

This study is not a script. It is a set of lenses -- ways of understanding the people God has placed in our lives so that we can speak the gospel with intelligence, sensitivity, and genuine love. We will look at five major worldviews that shape the people around us: the secular Western mind, and then four of the world's great faith traditions -- Judaism, Islam, Hinduism, and Buddhism. For each, we ask the same three questions: How do they see the world? Where does their worldview leave them without answers? And where is the natural bridge to the gospel of Jesus Christ?

The final unit draws it all together with the practical skills of a gospel conversation: how to ask good questions, how to listen well, how to move from everyday life to eternal things, and how to present Christ clearly and winsome1y. The goal throughout is not debate victory but genuine love -- the love of God for people he made, people he knows by name, people for whom Christ died.

Paul's words frame the whole study: 'I have become all things to all people, that by all means I might save some. I do it all for the sake of the gospel' (1 Cor. 9:22-23). This is not compromise; it is contextualisation -- the same gospel, spoken in a language each person can actually hear.

1.title: The Western Secular Mind
1.overview:
The person most of us interact with daily is not a committed atheist with a coherent philosophical system. They are something more elusive: a secular Westerner -- someone who has simply absorbed the assumption that the natural, material world is all there is, that morality is personal and relative, that the self is the highest authority, and that religion is at best a private comfort and at worst an embarrassing relic.

Carl Trueman's diagnosis is precise: modern Western culture is shaped by 'expressive individualism' -- the belief that the authentic self is found by looking inward, and that the primary moral obligation is to express that self freely. Identity is not received (from God, family, community, tradition) but self-constructed. The great virtues are authenticity and tolerance; the great sins are judgmentalism and exclusivity. Into this world, the gospel arrives sounding deeply strange: sin, judgment, atonement, resurrection -- these are not categories the secular mind reaches for.

And yet the secular worldview is full of cracks. It cannot account for the moral outrage it constantly expresses (why is anything truly wrong?). It cannot provide a satisfying answer to death. It cannot sustain the meaning it promises -- the 'good life' of the secular West is oddly joyless, anxious, and lonely. Tim Keller's approach is invaluable here: find the longing the secular worldview promises to satisfy but cannot, and show how the gospel addresses that longing at its root.

The bridge questions: Where do you find your sense of worth? What gives your life meaning? What do you do with guilt? What do you believe happens when you die?
1.theology: The doctrine of the imago Dei is the key to understanding secular longing. Every human being -- however post-Christian their worldview -- bears the image of God and cannot fully suppress it. The suppression of Romans 1 is real, but it is never total. The longing for transcendence, the rage against injustice, the hunger for meaning, the fear of death -- these are all echoes of the image. Pascal called it the 'God-shaped vacuum.' The apologist and evangelist alike learn to hear these echoes and to show the person that what they are reaching for has a name: the God who made them, the Christ who died for them, the Spirit who can fill what nothing else can.
1.examples: A young professional says she doesn't believe in God but volunteers at a homeless shelter every week because 'people matter.' She has unwittingly borrowed a Christian premise (human dignity) without its foundation (the imago Dei). The gentle question -- 'Why do they matter, if we are just the products of random processes?' -- is not an attack. It is an invitation to examine whether her own deepest convictions point beyond the worldview she has accepted. Many secular Westerners are one honest conversation away from discovering that what they already believe requires God to make sense of it.

verseByVerse.quote: So Paul, standing in the midst of the Areopagus, said: 'Men of Athens, I perceive that in every way you are very religious. For as I passed along and observed the objects of your worship, I found also an altar with this inscription: To the unknown god. What therefore you worship as unknown, this I proclaim to you.' (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul's Areopagus method is the model for secular engagement: he walks their city, observes their culture, finds the altar they have already built. The secular Westerner has altars too -- to self-fulfilment, to justice, to love, to legacy. Paul does not mock the altar; he uses it. 'What you worship as unknown, this I proclaim.' He starts where they are and moves to where they need to be. He quotes their poets (Acts 17:28). He earns the right to be heard before he asks to be believed.

verseByVerse.quote: For although they knew God, they did not honor him as God or give thanks to him, but they became futile in their thinking, and their foolish hearts were darkened. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The secular mind is not a mind that never knew God; it is a mind that knows God and turns away. The 'futility' Paul describes is the existential emptiness of a life lived without its proper centre. The secular person often experiences this -- as anxiety, purposelessness, the vague sense that something is missing -- but cannot name it. The evangelist names it gently: 'What you are feeling may be the distance between the life you were made for and the life you are living.' This is not condemnation; it is diagnosis.

verseByVerse.quote: Vanity of vanities, says the Preacher, vanity of vanities! All is vanity. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Ecclesiastes is perhaps the most useful book in the Bible for engaging the secular mind -- because it begins exactly where the secular mind lives. Qoheleth has tried everything the secular good life offers: pleasure, achievement, wealth, wisdom, relationships. His verdict: 'vanity' -- breath, mist, emptiness. The secular Westerner often knows this feeling, even if they have not read the Preacher. The book's journey from emptiness to the fear of God (Eccl. 12:13) mirrors the journey we invite the secular person to take.

verseByVerse.quote: The thief comes only to steal and kill and destroy. I came that they may have life and have it abundantly. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The gospel offer to the secular mind is not religion but life -- the life Jesus calls 'abundant.' This is not prosperity or ease; it is the fullness of existence lived in relationship with the God for whom we were made. When the secular person has exhausted the offerings of the culture and found them wanting, this offer is the most subversive thing they can hear: 'What if there is more? What if the emptiness is not the end of the story but the beginning of a better one?'

2.title: Jewish Friends
2.overview:
No relationship in evangelism carries more historical weight -- or more responsibility -- than our engagement with Jewish people. For two thousand years, the church has been guilty of horrific treatment of the Jewish people: the Crusades, forced conversions, pogroms, and ultimately the Holocaust, in a continent that called itself Christian. Before we open our mouths to speak the gospel to a Jewish person, we must be aware of this history and carry it with genuine grief. We are not starting from a neutral point; we are starting from a deep deficit of trust that only patient, respectful, loving relationship can begin to address.

And yet the gospel is first of all Jewish. Jesus was Jewish -- a rabbi from Galilee, a son of David, the fulfilment of Israel's story. The first Christians were Jewish. The New Testament is saturated with the Hebrew Scriptures. To share the gospel with a Jewish person is not to ask them to leave their heritage but to show them its completion. The Messiah they await has already come.

The key bridges: the suffering servant of Isaiah 53 (the most powerful single text for Jewish evangelism -- describe it without naming the chapter and ask who they think it describes); the Passover lamb and atonement without sacrifice (since the Temple's destruction in 70 AD, there is no sacrifice -- how is sin atoned for?); Daniel 9's timeline of the Messiah's coming; and Psalm 22's extraordinary detail of crucifixion written a thousand years before Rome invented it.

The great stumbling blocks: the Trinity (sounds like three gods), the suffering Messiah (many Jews expect a conquering king), and the church's history. Approach with patience, deep respect, and genuine love. Many Jewish people are secular and will respond first to the secular questions above. Messianic believers -- Jewish Christians -- are invaluable conversation partners and bridges.
2.theology: The covenant structure of the Old Testament is the theological key. God's covenant with Abraham (Gen. 12, 15, 17) is the foundation on which all of Scripture's story rests. The New Covenant (Jer. 31:31-34) is not the abolition of the Abrahamic covenant but its fulfilment -- the law written on the heart, full forgiveness of sins, God dwelling with his people. Jesus is the seed of Abraham through whom all nations are blessed (Gal. 3:16), the true Israel who does what Israel could not do (Matt. 2-5), the Lamb who is the final Passover (1 Cor. 5:7). Paul's anguish for his Jewish kinsmen (Rom. 9:1-5) is the pastoral model: deep love, not superiority.
2.examples: A pastor in a mixed neighbourhood befriends a Jewish neighbour over months of normal life -- meals, sport, occasional conversation. When the neighbour asks why the pastor seems so genuinely at peace, the conversation opens. The pastor does not begin with theology; he begins with relationship. Over time, he reads Isaiah 53 with his friend and asks simply: 'Who do you think this is?' The question does its own work. This is the pattern: relationship first, patient Scripture engagement second, Spirit-wrought conviction third. There is no shortcut. There is also no more rewarding conversation in all of evangelism.

verseByVerse.quote: But he was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace, and with his wounds we are healed. All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned -- every one -- to his own way; and the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Isaiah 53 is the great evangelical text for Jewish engagement. Written 700 years before Christ, it describes with extraordinary precision the substitutionary suffering of a figure who bears the sins of others. The earliest rabbinic interpretations often identified this figure as the Messiah; later interpretation shifted to Israel as a collective. The evangelist's simple question -- 'Who do you think Isaiah is describing?' -- opens a conversation that the text itself drives. This is perhaps the single most powerful passage of Scripture for Jewish evangelism.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and the house of Judah... I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts. And I will be their God, and they shall be my people... I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: God himself promised a New Covenant -- not a replacement of Israel but a deepening of God's relationship with his people. The New Covenant's three marks are: the law internalized (not just external commands but transformed hearts), intimate knowledge of God ('all shall know me'), and full forgiveness of sin. Jesus, at the Last Supper, identifies his blood as 'the blood of the new covenant' (Matt. 26:28). The New Covenant is not Christianity replacing Judaism; it is God's ancient promise to Israel finding its fulfilment.

verseByVerse.quote: I am speaking the truth in Christ -- I am not lying; my conscience bears me witness in the Holy Spirit -- that I have great sorrow and unceasing anguish in my heart. For I could wish that I myself were accursed and cut off from Christ for the sake of my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul's model for Jewish evangelism is love to the point of anguish. He does not engage his Jewish kinsmen with triumphalism or superiority; he engages them with a broken heart. He lists their privileges -- the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the law, the worship, the promises, the patriarchs -- with deep pride and grief. The tone of genuine Jewish evangelism must be this: not 'you have got it wrong' but 'I have found the One your whole story was pointing to, and I long for you to know him too.'

verseByVerse.quote: For dogs encompass me; a company of evildoers encircles me; they have pierced my hands and feet -- I can count all my bones -- they stare and gloat over me; they divide my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Psalm 22 is David's prayer of desolation -- and its details describe crucifixion with uncanny precision: pierced hands and feet, bones out of joint, parching thirst, garments divided by lot. Jesus quoted its opening line from the cross (Matt. 27:46). Crucifixion was not a Jewish form of execution and would not have been in David's cultural imagination. The Psalm points forward to one who would suffer precisely this way. Offered carefully in conversation, this text raises a question that is worth sitting with: 'Who is this?'

3.title: Muslim Friends
3.overview:
Islam is the world's fastest-growing religion and a significant presence in most Western cities. Muslims are often our neighbours, colleagues, and friends -- and many are far more spiritually serious than the average secular Westerner. They pray five times a day. They fast. They give to the poor. They take God seriously. This seriousness is to be respected, not patronised.

The Muslim worldview rests on several key convictions: tawhid (the absolute oneness and transcendence of God -- the greatest sin is shirk, associating anything with God); Muhammad as the final prophet and the Quran as the final, uncorrupted revelation; the five pillars of practice; and salvation by works -- at death, a person's deeds are weighed, and Allah decides. There is no assurance of paradise except for martyrs. This last point is often the most striking to Muslims themselves: they live without certainty of God's acceptance.

The key bridges: (1) The love of God -- Islam emphasizes God's power and mercy, but the Quran does not say 'God is love' (1 John 4:8). The idea of a God who loves unconditionally, who pursues the lost, who gives himself for sinners, is startling and beautiful. (2) Assurance -- 'Can you know that God has accepted you?' opens a genuine longing. (3) The cross -- Muslims are taught that Jesus did not die (someone else died in his place); gently engaging the historical evidence for the crucifixion is important here.

The key stumbling blocks: the Trinity (Muslims believe Christians worship three gods -- patiently clarify: one God, three persons; God is not lonely, he is love within himself); Jesus as Son of God (Muslims hear this biologically -- patiently clarify it as a title of relationship and divine nature, not physical sonship); the reliability of the Bible (Muslims believe it has been corrupted -- the manuscript evidence is a powerful response).
3.theology: The doctrine of atonement is the sharpest contrast between Islam and Christianity. In Islam, God forgives by decree -- he simply decides to overlook sin. The problem is that this makes God's forgiveness arbitrary and his justice questionable: sin is never actually dealt with, just waived. The Christian gospel insists that God is both just and the justifier (Rom. 3:26) -- that the cross is the place where divine justice and divine mercy meet. God does not simply overlook sin; he bears it himself in Christ. This is simultaneously the greatest stumbling block for Muslim understanding and the greatest gift the gospel has to offer: a forgiveness that is both free and just.
3.examples: A Muslim student in a university dorm conversation asks a Christian friend: 'How can you be sure you are going to heaven?' The Christian friend says: 'Because my confidence is not in my deeds but in what Christ has done. He took the penalty I deserved. My certainty is in him, not in myself.' The student is quiet for a moment. 'We do not have that,' he says. 'We never know.' The conversation that follows is one of the most significant either of them will have. The question of assurance opens a door that theological argument rarely can. Many Muslims have been reached not through debate but through the attractive fragrance of a Christian who is genuinely at peace with God.

verseByVerse.quote: Anyone who does not love does not know God, because God is love. In this the love of God was made manifest among us, that God sent his only Son into the world, so that we might live through him. In this is love, not that we have loved God but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The statement 'God is love' -- not merely 'God is loving' but God is love in his very being -- is one of the most distinctive claims of Christian theology, with no parallel in Islam. The Trinity makes this possible: within the eternal Godhead, the Father has loved the Son and the Son has loved the Father, in the Spirit, from before creation. Love is not a response to us; it is God's own eternal nature. When a Muslim friend grasps this -- that the God of the universe is, at his core, love -- something often shifts. This God is not merely to be obeyed; he can be known.

verseByVerse.quote: It was to show his righteousness at the present time, so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The gospel solves a problem that Islamic theology does not fully reckon with: how can a just God forgive sinners without compromising his justice? Islam says God forgives by will -- he simply decides to pardon. But this leaves the question of justice unresolved. The gospel says God is 'just and the justifier' -- both at once, simultaneously, without contradiction, because Christ bore the penalty in our place. The cross is God's justice satisfied and God's mercy expressed in the same moment. This is the heart of the gospel that Islam does not have.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to him, 'I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me.' (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Muslims revere Jesus (Isa) as a great prophet -- virgin-born, miracle-working, and coming again in the last days. The Quran gives him remarkable titles. The question the evangelist raises is: is this Jesus -- who claimed to be the way, the truth, and the life; who forgave sins (a prerogative of God alone); who said 'Before Abraham was, I am' (John 8:58) -- simply a prophet? Or is he something more? The Muslim view of Jesus as a prophet has difficulty accounting for these claims. A prophet does not say 'no one comes to the Father except through me.'

verseByVerse.quote: And he arose and came to his father. But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The parable of the prodigal son has been used powerfully in Muslim evangelism -- because it presents a picture of God that Islam does not offer: a father who runs to the returning sinner, who does not wait to weigh the merits of the return, who interrupts the prepared speech of repentance with an embrace and a feast. In Middle Eastern culture, a man of honour does not run -- it is beneath his dignity. The father runs. This is the scandal of grace. Many Muslim friends, hearing this story for the first time, are moved to tears. The God who runs is a God they have never been told about.

4.title: Hindu Friends
4.overview:
Hinduism is extraordinarily diverse -- it encompasses sophisticated philosophical monism (Advaita Vedanta: all is Brahman, the individual self is an illusion), popular polytheism (millions of devas/gods), devotional theism (bhakti yoga, personal devotion to a deity such as Vishnu or Krishna), and ethical frameworks (dharma, caste). This diversity means there is no single 'Hindu' to engage; you must listen carefully to the specific tradition and emphasis of the person in front of you.

Some common threads: karma (the moral law of cause and effect -- every action has consequences that carry forward, including into future lives); samsara (the cycle of rebirth driven by karma); moksha (liberation from the cycle -- the ultimate goal, whether understood as union with Brahman, release of the individual soul, or eternal communion with a personal god); and the idea that all paths lead to the same ultimate reality (sarva dharma samabhava -- all religions are equal paths).

The key bridges: (1) The personal God -- many Hindus, especially those in the bhakti tradition, long for a personal relationship with a God who knows and loves them. The Christian God -- who calls us by name, who became flesh, who says 'I am with you always' -- speaks directly to this longing. (2) Karma vs. grace -- karma is relentless: every action creates debt that must be worked off through suffering and rebirth. The gospel offers something karma cannot: the cancellation of debt, not by working it off but by having it borne by another. Grace is the most revolutionary concept in the Hindu's world. (3) The resurrection -- Hinduism offers escape from the cycle; Christianity offers the transformation of the cycle. The resurrection is not absorption into Brahman but the restoration of the embodied self in a new creation.

The key stumbling block: the all-paths-lead-to-God view. Engage it gently: 'Do all paths really lead to the same place? The God of the Bible says he is love; some Hindu systems say the individual self does not ultimately exist. These are not the same God or the same goal -- can they both be true at the same time?'
4.theology: The doctrine of grace is the sharpest theological contrast with Hinduism. Karma is an impersonal, inexorable moral law: you reap what you sow, across lifetimes, without exception and without mercy. Grace is its antithesis: the free, unearned cancellation of debt by a personal God who chooses to absorb the consequence himself. 'For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast' (Eph. 2:8-9). In a karmic framework, this is literally unthinkable -- you cannot simply cancel karma; it must be worked out. The gospel's announcement that the karmic debt has been paid by Christ, once for all, is both staggering and beautiful.
4.examples: A Hindu colleague asks a Christian friend why she is so generous -- she gives her time, her money, her attention freely, without any obvious personal benefit. The friend explains: 'I do it because I have been given everything I have by a God who loves me. I am just passing on what I have received. I am not trying to accumulate good karma -- I am responding to grace already given.' The concept of acting not to accumulate merit but to respond to love already received is genuinely foreign to the karmic framework -- and genuinely attractive. Many Hindus have begun their journey toward Christ not through an argument but through observing a life lived in grace.

verseByVerse.quote: For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: In a karmic worldview, salvation (moksha) is always the result of accumulated merit -- good deeds, devotion, right knowledge -- across potentially millions of lifetimes. The gospel's announcement is revolutionary: salvation is a gift. Not earned, not accumulated, not the result of spiritual effort, but freely given to the one who simply receives it by faith. The person trapped in the exhausting logic of karma -- never knowing if they have done enough, never sure of their standing -- hears in these words an invitation to rest. 'It is not your doing.' Three of the most liberating words in any language.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to her, 'Everyone who drinks of this water will be thirsty again, but whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never be thirsty again. The water that I will give him will become in him a spring of water welling up to eternal life.' (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus' conversation with the Samaritan woman -- a woman of mixed religious heritage -- models cross-cultural evangelism beautifully. He meets her at her point of daily need (water), addresses her deepest relational thirst (five husbands, still searching), and offers something that satisfies permanently. The Hindu journey through samsara is a journey of recurring thirst -- each life offering temporary satisfaction before the cycle begins again. Jesus offers water that ends the thirst permanently. Not another life, but life itself.

verseByVerse.quote: ...knowing that you were ransomed from the futile ways inherited from your forefathers, not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The word 'ransomed' speaks directly to the karmic debt. A ransom is paid to free someone from a debt they cannot pay themselves. Christ has paid the ransom -- not in gold or spiritual effort, but in his own blood. 'Futile ways inherited from your forefathers' resonates with the Hindu sense of ancestral obligation and generational karma. The gospel announces that the inherited debt has been cancelled, that the cycle has been broken, not by superior spiritual achievement but by the precious blood of the one who entered the cycle himself and broke it from within.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to her, 'I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live, and everyone who lives and believes in me shall never die.' (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The Hindu goal is release from the cycle of rebirth -- the dissolution of individual identity into Brahman, like a drop returning to the ocean. The resurrection offers something radically different: not the dissolution of the self but its transformation and restoration. Jesus does not offer escape from embodied existence; he offers its glorification. 'I am the resurrection' -- a resurrection, not an absorption. The individual is not lost in God; the individual is fully known by God, fully loved by God, and fully raised by God. You are not a drop returning to the ocean; you are a child coming home to a Father.

5.title: Buddhist Friends
5.overview:
Buddhism, in its classical form, is both profound and, from a Christian perspective, deeply alien. The Buddha's diagnosis of the human condition is sharp: life is characterized by dukkha (suffering/unsatisfactoriness), caused by tanha (craving/attachment). The solution is the Eightfold Path -- a disciplined practice of right thought, right action, right mindfulness -- leading to the cessation of craving and ultimately to nirvana (literally 'blowing out' -- the extinguishing of the self that craves). Most Buddhist schools teach anatta (no permanent self) -- there is no soul, no enduring identity, only a stream of consciousness and experience. And there is no creator God in classical Buddhism -- the universe is beginningless and lawful, not created.

In the West, Buddhism is often encountered in a much softer form: mindfulness practices, compassion ethics, and a general orientation toward inner peace, stripped of the metaphysical framework. This 'mindfulness Buddhism' is widespread, appealing, and often the gateway to questions about the fuller tradition.

The key bridges: (1) The problem of suffering -- the Buddhist diagnosis of dukkha resonates deeply with Christian honesty about the fallenness of the world. Both traditions take suffering seriously. But the Buddhist solution (extinguish the self that suffers) differs radically from the Christian solution (God enters the suffering and transforms it). (2) Compassion -- Mahayana Buddhism develops the bodhisattva ideal (one who delays their own nirvana to help others attain liberation). This is genuine compassion, but it faces a philosophical challenge: if there is no self, why does the suffering of others matter? The Christian answer -- every person bears the image of God, and God himself is love -- grounds compassion in a way that no-self philosophy cannot. (3) The resurrection -- Buddhism offers escape from existence; Christ offers the renewal of existence. The self is not destroyed but restored.

Approach with genuine interest. Buddhism is a serious, ancient, sophisticated tradition. Many Buddhists have thought more carefully about suffering and the nature of mind than most Christians have. Listen, respect, and then share the difference that the resurrection of Jesus Christ makes.
5.theology: The Christian doctrine of the imago Dei is the theological answer to anatta (no-self). Human beings are not streams of consciousness with no enduring identity; they are image-bearers of a personal God, known by name, loved individually, and destined for personal resurrection. This is both the sharpest theological contrast with Buddhism and the most pastorally significant: 'You are not nothing. You are someone -- someone God made, someone God loves, someone Christ died for, someone the Spirit indwells.' The Buddhist no-self teaching, however philosophically sophisticated, cannot ultimately sustain the compassion it extols -- because compassion requires a real self to do the caring and a real self to receive the care.
5.examples: A Christian friend of a Buddhist colleague notices that the colleague speaks constantly about compassion -- for animals, for the environment, for the suffering poor. One day the friend asks: 'I love that you care so much. Can I ask -- why do you think others' suffering matters? If there is no permanent self, no God, no objective purpose -- why should I care about another stream of consciousness?' The Buddhist friend pauses. 'That is the question I have not been able to answer.' It is not a trick question; it is a genuine one. And the conversation that follows -- about the God who is love, who made the other person in his image, who himself suffered for them -- goes places that neither of them expected.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The Beatitudes resonate in the Buddhist world because they begin where Buddhism begins: with an honest acknowledgement of human poverty and suffering. But the Beatitudes do not counsel detachment -- they counsel hope. 'They shall be comforted' is a future promise from a God who acts. Buddhism addresses suffering by eliminating the self that suffers; the Beatitudes address suffering by promising that a God who is there will comfort the sufferer. These are very different responses to the same honest diagnosis. The Buddhist who hears the Beatitudes often recognizes both the shared diagnosis and the very different cure.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus wept. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The shortest verse in the Bible is one of the most powerful for Buddhist engagement. At Lazarus's tomb, facing the suffering of Mary and Martha, the Son of God weeps. Not because he does not know the resurrection is coming (he does -- he is about to perform it). But because he is moved by the grief of those he loves. This is not the detachment that Buddhism commends; it is the opposite -- full, painful, compassionate engagement with the suffering of others. The Christian God does not transcend suffering by rising above it; he enters it. The cross is God weeping at the ultimate tomb -- and then opening it.

verseByVerse.quote: For the creation was subjected to futility, not willingly, but because of him who subjected it, in hope that the creation itself will be set free from its bondage to corruption and obtain the freedom of the glory of the children of God. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The Buddhist diagnosis -- the world is characterized by dukkha, impermanence, and suffering -- finds a surprisingly sympathetic echo in Paul's words: creation has been 'subjected to futility,' it groans. But Paul's response differs entirely: not escape from creation but its liberation. The creation itself will be 'set free' and 'obtain the freedom of the glory of the children of God.' This is resurrection applied cosmically -- not the dissolution of the world into nothingness but its transformation into something gloriously new. Buddhism says: escape the wheel. The gospel says: the wheel is being remade.

verseByVerse.quote: For 'In him we live and move and have our being'; as even some of your own poets have said, 'For we are indeed his offspring.' (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul quotes a Greek poet (Aratus) whose words resonate in the Buddhist world: we exist within and through a greater reality. But Paul identifies that reality as a personal God -- not an impersonal ground of being, not a principle of dharma, but 'him' in whom we live and move. The personal pronoun is everything. In classical Buddhism, the ultimate reality (if there is one) is impersonal. The gospel announces that ultimate reality is a Person -- and that persons are therefore ultimate. The Buddhist intuition that we are connected to something greater is correct; the gospel reveals what that something is: not Brahman, not dharma, but the Father of Jesus Christ.

6.title: The Gospel Conversation: Asking, Listening, Sharing
6.overview:
Everything in this study has been preparation for a conversation. Not a lecture, not a debate, not a presentation -- a conversation. Two human beings, made in the image of God, talking honestly about the things that matter most. The best evangelists are not the most eloquent speakers; they are the most attentive listeners. They ask good questions, give the other person room to think out loud, and trust that the Spirit is already at work in the person long before they arrived.

The art of the gospel conversation has three movements: asking, listening, and sharing.

Asking: good evangelistic questions open the person up rather than shutting them down. 'What do you believe about...' is better than 'Have you heard of...'. 'What gives your life meaning?' is better than 'Do you know you are a sinner?' Questions like: 'What do you make of Jesus?', 'If there is a God, what do you think he is like?', 'What happens when we die?', 'What do you do with guilt?' -- these are questions that almost anyone will engage with, and they all point toward the gospel.

Listening: really listening -- not loading your reply while they speak -- communicates respect, love, and genuine interest. It also tells you what the person actually believes, as opposed to what you assumed they believe. The person who feels genuinely heard is far more open to hearing in return.

Sharing: when the moment comes to share the gospel, keep it clear and personal. What is the problem (we are separated from God by sin)? What is the solution (Christ died for us and rose again)? What is the response (repent and trust him)? And then -- your own story. Not a polished testimony, but genuine and personal: 'This is what changed for me. This is why I believe this is true.'

And then trust the Spirit. You plant and water. God gives the growth.
6.theology: The doctrine of prevenient (preceding) grace -- in Reformed thought, better described as the Spirit's convicting and drawing work prior to conversion (John 16:8-11) -- means that the evangelist never enters a conversation as the first to arrive. The Spirit has been at work in the person before we got there. He has been using beauty, suffering, conscience, relationship, and the echoes of the imago Dei to prepare the ground. Our role is to name what is already happening, to be faithful witnesses, and to trust the One whose job conversion actually is. This liberates us from performance anxiety: we are not responsible for the result. We are responsible for faithfulness.
6.examples: A woman shares her faith with a colleague for two years -- coffee conversations, honest questions, occasional pushback. She never gives up, never becomes preachy, never stops being genuinely interested in her colleague's life. One day the colleague says: 'I have been thinking about what you said about Jesus. Can we talk more seriously?' She had been prepared over two years of faithful, patient, loving relationship. The gospel seed had been sown in dozens of small conversations -- not a single dramatic presentation. Most people do not come to faith through a stranger at a stall; they come through the sustained witness of someone who genuinely loves them. Be that person. The harvest belongs to God; the faithfulness belongs to you.

verseByVerse.quote: Walk in wisdom toward outsiders, making the best use of the time. Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt, so that you may know how you ought to answer each person. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul's evangelism instruction is relational and contextual. 'Walk in wisdom toward outsiders' -- the posture comes before the speech. 'Making the best use of the time' -- noticing and seizing the moments that open. 'Gracious, seasoned with salt' -- both nourishing and interesting; both true and attractive. 'How you ought to answer each person' -- not one-size-fits-all, but discerningly fitted to the individual. This is why we have studied different worldviews: so that our speech to each person is seasoned with the right flavour, meeting them where they actually are.

verseByVerse.quote: I have become all things to all people, that by all means I might save some. I do it all for the sake of the gospel, that I may share with them in its blessings. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul's great evangelistic principle: adapt the approach without altering the message. He does not say 'I have changed the gospel for all people.' He says 'I have become all things' -- changed his cultural approach, his starting point, his relational posture. With Jews he engaged on the Law and the prophets. With Greeks he quoted their poets. With the weak he was weak. The gospel remains constant; the bridge is built with whatever material is at hand in the listener's world. Contextualisation is not compromise; it is love in action.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he comes, he will convict the world concerning sin and righteousness and judgment. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The Spirit's job description for evangelism. He convicts -- not us. We witness; he convicts. We speak; he opens hearts. We plant and water; he gives the growth. This is the evangelist's great liberation: you are not responsible for the outcome. You are responsible for faithfulness. The Spirit was at work in the person before you met them, and he will continue his work long after the conversation ends. Your role is to be a faithful, loving, clear witness. The rest belongs to him.

verseByVerse.quote: For I delivered to you as of first importance what I also received: that Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day in accordance with the Scriptures. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: When the moment comes to share the gospel -- whatever worldview the person comes from, whatever the bridge has been -- this is the message. Not a technique, not a system, but a fact: Christ died for our sins. He was buried. He was raised. These are historical claims about real events with real consequences. The gospel is not advice ('try this approach to life'); it is news ('something has happened that changes everything'). And it is news for everyone -- secular Westerner, Jewish friend, Muslim neighbour, Hindu colleague, Buddhist acquaintance. Christ died for sins. He is risen. Come and see.
